passage:
At ten, Payal found the wind-up robot snapped in two on the floor and rounded on Omkar, Payal's younger brother. "You did this on purpose!" Omkar stood with wet cheeks and hands behind his back. Payal's fists were tight, but then Payal saw his small shoulders shaking and understood that Omkar was afraid of being told off, not pleased with himself. "I'll say it fell," Payal said stiffly, still cross.

At fifteen, Payal came home late from rehearsal, and Jaya, Payal's mother, met Payal at the door. "Why didn't you call? Anything could have happened!" Payal said Jaya trusted nobody, slammed the bedroom door and lay there sure that only one side made sense. An hour later Payal noticed the strip of light under the door and the plate of dinner left beside it, and remembered how Jaya's voice had cracked. Payal carried the plate to the kitchen. "Sorry I didn't call. You were scared, weren't you?"

qa.q: What had happened to the wind-up robot?
qa.a: The wind-up robot was snapped in two on the floor.

qa.q: How does Payal's view of the other person change between the broken robot and the door-slamming quarrel?
qa.a: At ten Payal shouts at Omkar but then sees his shaking shoulders and knows he is afraid of being told off. At fifteen, in the quarrel with Jaya, Payal sees only one side until an hour later, when the plate left by the door shows Jaya's fear. Seeing another's view is real but effortful, and anger narrows it until calm returns.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling while lying behind the slammed door?
qa.a: Payal felt angry and certain of being right, so the view was narrowed to Payal's own side.

qa.q: What could Payal do next to keep the understanding from fading?
qa.a: Payal could tell Jaya how late the rehearsal ran and agree on a quick call next time, so both are less scared.

grounding: A child sees a sibling's fear behind a broken toy and a teen only later sees a parent's fear behind a quarrel, showing perspective-taking that emotion narrows.
